title: 1 Effect of supplemental protein degradability on nitrogen metabolism and performance of beef steers grazing dormant tallgrass prairie
content:
Abstract
Protein is often the first nutrient that is limited in diets of growing calves on low quality forage diets. Therefore, nitrogen utilization is vital to optimize nutrition of beef calves grazing dormant native range. The objective of this study was to determine the effects of supplements containing low or high proportions of rumen degradable protein (RDP) on nitrogen utilization while cattle were grazing dormant tallgrass prairie. Weaned and preconditioned beef steers (n = 23; BW = 302 ± 8.2 kg) grazed dormant tallgrass prairie for 85 days. Steers were randomly assigned to either a high RDP, or high rumen undegradable protein (RUP) supplement at 6.36 kg/week prorated for feeding three times weekly. Supplements consisted of wheat middlings, and soybean meal for RDP supplement and wheat middlings, and corn gluten meal for RUP supplements. Steers were gathered from a single tallgrass prairie pasture at 0800 each Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday placed into individual feeding stations and provided their respective supplement before returning to pasture. Blood, urine, and fecal samples were collected on days 0, 42, 63, and 84 for nitrogen analysis. Fecal samples were serially collected on day 46 to 50 and day 67 to 71 in 4-hour increments to measure passage rate using titanium dioxide and yttrium as pulse dosed external markers. Forage masticate samples were collected on d 50 and day 71 following rumen evacuation of a ruminally cannulated steer that had been grazing with study steers. Body weights (BW) were collected full with no previous shrink on days 0, 1, 29, 42, 63, 84, 85, and 145 for performance measurements. Data were analyzed as a completely random design experiment using the mixed models procedure of SAS (SAS Inst. Inc., Cary NC) with treatment as the fixed effect and steer the experimental unit. Steers in the RUP treatment group were 8.2 kg heavier (P = 0.03) than the RDP treatment group steers at the conclusion of the study. The difference in BW at the end of supplementation is because the steers in RUP treatment lost 0.2 kg less BW/d (P < 0.01) than the RDP steers, while grazing dormant range. Following the completion of the study, when steers were grazing early spring regrowth with ad libitum bermuda grass hay without supplementation, the RDP treatment steers had improved gain (P = 0.04) during the remaining 60 days prior to shipping, but compensated for only 33% of the BW difference at the end of the supplementation period. Steers fed a high RUP supplement while grazing dormant range recycled adequate protein to meet supplementation requirements and improve performance compared with the RDP supplement.
